assignments.title: Critical Questions: Webster's Seventh of March Speech (1850)
assignments.html:
MODULE 5 · CRITICAL QUESTIONS
Critical Questions: Webster's Seventh of March Speech (1850)
10 points · written answers · one turn-in
✦ ✧ ✦
Instructions

Read the primary source for this week: Daniel Webster's Seventh of March Speech. Then answer both questions in your own words. Aim for four to six sentences each.

Your answers are already in My Notebook from the lessons. Copy each one into your submission under its question number, and finish any you left blank.

  1. Suppose Webster had opposed Clay's plan instead of supporting it. How might the Senate vote and the Compromise of 1850 have turned out, and why?
  2. Many people in New England felt betrayed by Webster, yet he said he spoke "not as a Massachusetts man, nor as a Northern man, but as an American." Why does the choice he made matter for how Americans later thought about their duties to the Union?

How to submit: type both answers in the text box, numbering them 1 and 2. This assignment is graded on effort and thinking: a complete, thoughtful answer to both questions earns full credit.

assignments.title: Primary Source Exercise: Douglass, "What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?" (1852)
assignments.html:
MODULE 5 · PRIMARY SOURCE EXERCISE
Primary Source Exercise: Douglass, "What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?" (1852)
10 points · written answers · one turn-in
✦ ✧ ✦
Instructions

Read the primary source: part of Frederick Douglass's speech "What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?" Then answer both questions in your own words, in four to six sentences each.

Your answers are already in My Notebook from the lessons. Copy each one into your submission under its question number, and finish any you left blank.

  1. Douglass gave this speech to people gathered to celebrate American independence. Why does it matter that he spoke on that occasion and to that audience?
  2. Suppose Douglass had agreed with Garrison that the Constitution was a proslavery document. How might his speech and his advice to his listeners have been different?

How to submit: type both answers in the text box, numbering them 1 and 2. This assignment is graded on effort and thinking: a complete, thoughtful answer to both questions earns full credit.

assignments.title: Critical Questions: Taney's Opinion in Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857)
assignments.html:
MODULE 5 · CRITICAL QUESTIONS
Critical Questions: Taney's Opinion in Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857)
10 points · written answers · one turn-in
✦ ✧ ✦
Instructions

Read the primary source for this week: an excerpt from Chief Justice Taney's opinion in Dred Scott v. Sandford. Then answer both questions in your own words. Aim for four to six sentences each.

Your answers are already in My Notebook from the lessons. Copy each one into your submission under its question number, and finish any you left blank.

  1. Taney wrote that no Black person could be a citizen and that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories. Using the opinion and the lesson Douglas Attempts a New Compromise, explain what events before 1857 led many Americans to hope that the Court could settle the slavery question.
  2. Suppose the Court had decided only that Dred Scott's stay in a free state did not make him free, and had not ruled on Congress's power over the territories. How might the political fight have changed, and why?

How to submit: type both answers in the text box, numbering them 1 and 2. This assignment is graded on effort and thinking: a complete, thoughtful answer to both questions earns full credit.

Primary Source Report: Lincoln's House Divided Speech (1858)
16 points · Word document · one turn-in
✦ ✧ ✦
Instructions

Read Abraham Lincoln's House Divided Speech. Then write a response of 250 to 400 words in a Word document that answers both questions below. Use your own words and refer to the source and to the lessons.

  1. What events between 1854 and 1858 led Lincoln to say that the country could not go on permanently half slave and half free?
  2. Suppose Lincoln had left the House Divided passage out of his speech to avoid losing votes. How might the 1858 campaign and his later career have been different, and why?

Your teacher will score your report with the rubric attached to this assignment: understanding of the material, quality of reasoning, clarity and precision of expression, and intellectual honesty. Intellectual honesty means telling what the source cannot show or what you are still unsure about.

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz: Lessons 4.4 and 5.1
quizzes.description:
MODULE 5 · READING QUIZ
Reading Quiz: Clay and Webster Compromise on California and Abolitionists Rouse the Public
7 questions · 7 points · 2 attempts
✦ ✧ ✦
Before you start

This quiz covers Clay and Webster Compromise on California and Abolitionists Rouse the Public. You may take it twice, and your higher score counts. Some questions ask you to put two or more facts together, so think before you answer.

questions.text: California's request to join the Union as a free state worried the South. Why?

answers.text: California had too few people to become a state.
The South wanted California to be divided into two states.
It would give the free states a 16 to 15 majority in the Senate for the first time, ending the balance held since 1820.
President Taylor was against admitting any new state.

questions.text: President Taylor's sudden death in July 1850 mattered to the Compromise of 1850. Why?

answers.text: His death meant the Senate had to be reelected.
His successor, Fillmore, supported the compromise, while Taylor had opposed Clay's approach.
Taylor had written the compromise himself.
Taylor's death ended the Mexican War.

questions.text: Which part of the Compromise of 1850 did the South want most, and why did it cause trouble in the North?

answers.text: The ban on the slave trade in Washington, D.C., because it closed Northern markets.
The admission of California, because it had gold.
The payment of Texas's debts, because it raised Northern taxes.
The stronger Fugitive Slave Act, because it required officials in every state to help return escaped slaves, drawing Northerners into slavery.

questions.text: After the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, thousands of free Black people in Northern cities left for Canada. What best explains this?

answers.text: The accused person could not testify, so free Black people feared being seized by mistake.
Canada had promised free land to everyone who came.
Congress ordered all free Black people to leave the North.
The Act applied only to people born in Canada.

questions.text: How did Frederick Douglass's view of the Constitution differ from William Lloyd Garrison's?

answers.text: Both thought the Constitution should be burned.
Garrison thought it should be amended; Douglass thought it should be ignored.
Garrison thought the Constitution was proslavery, while Douglass came to believe that, rightly read, it was antislavery and urged people to use politics.
Douglass thought slavery would end by itself.

questions.text: Which statement about the Underground Railroad is best supported by the lesson?

answers.text: It was a railroad built under the ground in Philadelphia.
It was a network of free Black people, white abolitionists, and churches, although most escapes were not organized by any network.
It was run entirely by the federal government.
It ended with the Fugitive Slave Act.

questions.text: Northern states passed personal liberty laws that made it harder to return a fugitive. Why did this make Southerners distrust compromise?

answers.text: Southerners believed the laws were unconstitutional but were happy to follow them.
Southerners wanted Northern states to leave the Union.
Southerners no longer owned any slaves.
Southerners had once argued that a state could refuse a federal law, and now Northern states were doing the same, so why trust any compromise?

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz: Lessons 5.2 and 5.3
quizzes.description:
MODULE 5 · READING QUIZ
Reading Quiz: Douglas Attempts a New Compromise and Lincoln Pledges to Unify the Country Around Freedom
7 questions · 7 points · 2 attempts
✦ ✧ ✦
Before you start

This quiz covers Douglas Attempts a New Compromise and Lincoln Pledges to Unify the Country Around Freedom. You may take it twice, and your higher score counts. Some questions ask you to put two or more facts together, so think before you answer.

questions.text: Why did Douglas agree to repeal the Missouri Compromise ban on slavery in the Kansas-Nebraska Act?

answers.text: Southern senators would not vote to organize the territories, which his railroad plan needed, unless the ban came off.
The Supreme Court had ordered the ban removed.
President Pierce wrote the repeal himself.
Kansas and Nebraska had already voted to allow slavery.

questions.text: Why did the Kansas-Nebraska Act lead to the founding of the Republican Party?

answers.text: Southern Democrats wanted a new party to protect slavery.
The Whig Party won every election in 1854.
Douglas started the party so he could run for President.
Many Northerners felt a promise of thirty-four years was broken to help slaveholders, so Whigs, Free Soilers, and antislavery Democrats formed a party to stop slavery from spreading.

questions.text: After the Dred Scott decision, Republicans said it made their whole program illegal. Why?

answers.text: It said that Republicans could not hold office.
If Congress could not ban slavery in the territories, then keeping slavery out of the territories, their main goal, was not allowed.
It forbade any new political parties.
It said the Republican Party was a Southern party.

questions.text: Preston Brooks beat Senator Sumner with a cane, and many Southerners sent Brooks new canes. What does this episode best show?

answers.text: Both sections strongly condemned the act.
Congress passed a law protecting senators.
The sections no longer saw the same events in the same way.
Sumner had started the fight with his fists.

questions.text: Which statement best describes Lincoln's position on slavery in 1858?

answers.text: He believed the Constitution protected slavery in the states where it existed, but he wanted to stop its spread and put it on a course of ultimate extinction.
He wanted to end slavery everywhere at once, as Garrison did.
He believed slavery should spread to every territory.
He had no opinion about slavery.

questions.text: Douglas's Freeport answer helped him win in Illinois but hurt him with Southern Democrats. Why?

answers.text: He said that slavery should be banned in all states.
He admitted that he had voted against Dred Scott.
He told the Court to resign.
He said settlers could keep slavery out by refusing to pass local laws to protect it, which seemed to ignore the Court's ruling.

questions.text: Lincoln said, "A house divided against itself cannot stand." What did he actually predict?

answers.text: That the Union would break apart within a year.
That the country could not remain permanently half slave and half free, and would become all one thing or all the other.
That the South would win the next election.
That slavery would end in the territories by itself.

quizzes.description:
MODULE 5 · READING QUIZ
Reading Quiz: John Brown Pronounces Divine Judgment on Slavery and South Carolina Leads the South Out of the Union
7 questions · 7 points · 2 attempts
✦ ✧ ✦
Before you start

This quiz covers John Brown Pronounces Divine Judgment on Slavery and South Carolina Leads the South Out of the Union. You may take it twice, and your higher score counts. Some questions ask you to put two or more facts together, so think before you answer.

questions.text: Frederick Douglass argued against John Brown's plan to raid Harpers Ferry. What was his reason?

answers.text: He believed slavery was not wrong.
He thought Harpers Ferry was a trap where Brown would be surrounded.
He had already joined the raid.
He wanted the raid to take place in Kansas.

questions.text: Southern newspapers asked whether Northerners who praised Brown could be trusted. Which fact could a Republican such as Lincoln point to in reply?

answers.text: Lincoln said that all slave owners should be punished.
Lincoln told Brown to start a rebellion.
Lincoln said that slavery was not wrong.
Lincoln said Brown was right to think slavery wrong, but that this could not excuse violence, bloodshed, and treason, and that votes were the way to end slavery.

questions.text: Why did Brown's raid make a war easier to imagine, even though it did not start one?

answers.text: It frightened the South, which saw a Northern man try to start an uprising praised by Northern writers, and Southern states raised militias.
It ended in a victory for the raiders.
It caused the Marines to leave the army.
It was supported by President Buchanan.

questions.text: The Democratic Party split in 1860. Why was this so important?

answers.text: It meant that no one ran against Lincoln.
It meant that the Democrats had ended slavery.
It was the one party that reached across the sections, and its split helped Lincoln win.
It forced Lincoln to give up the election.

questions.text: Lincoln won in 1860 with about 40 percent of the popular vote and not a single Southern electoral vote. What does this show?

answers.text: The South had voted for Lincoln in secret.
The Constitution was changed before the election.
The popular vote was ignored by law.
The North held most of the nation's electoral votes, and the Democratic split helped him, so the South could now be outvoted.

questions.text: Lincoln promised not to interfere with slavery where it already existed. Why did Southern leaders still distrust him?

answers.text: His party believed slavery was wrong and had won the White House without a Southern vote, so they feared the government would one day work to end slavery everywhere.
He had said that he would end slavery on his first day in office.
He had refused to speak to any Southerner.
He was born in the North.

questions.text: A student says that Virginia was among the first states to leave the Union. Which fact shows the student is wrong?

answers.text: Virginia voted 169 to 0 to leave on December 20, 1860.
Virginia never held a convention.
Seven Deep South states, including Florida, left between December 1860 and February 1861, while Virginia and the rest of the Upper South hesitated.
Virginia was the first state to join the Confederacy.

discussions.title: Discussion: Webster's Seventh of March Speech, Statesmanship or Surrender?

MODULE 5 · DISCUSSION
Discussion: Webster's Seventh of March Speech, Statesmanship or Surrender?
10 points · written post and one reply · threaded discussion

The prompt

Webster supported the Compromise of 1850, including the Fugitive Slave Act, to keep the Union together. Many people in his own region called it a surrender. Make one specific claim: was his speech an act of statesmanship, a surrender, or something in between? Use at least one fact from this week's lessons or sources to back your claim, and explain why that fact supports it. Write about 100 to 150 words.

Then reply to one classmate (about 50 to 100 words). If you agree, strengthen their reasoning with a new fact. If you disagree, respectfully explain where their reasoning falls short.
